text: Carlo Francesco Cogrossi (5 July 1682 – 13 January 1769) was an Italian physician who was among the first to suggest the theory of contagium vivum that minute invisible parasitic living organisms were a cause of disease. This seemingly counterintuitive conclusion arises from the premise that Achilles must first reach the point where the tortoise started, by which time the tortoise will have moved ahead, and so on, ad infinitum. This infinite sequence of smaller and smaller intervals appears to prevent Achilles from ever catching up. The crux of the issue lay in the concept of an infinite series, which, until the advent of modern mathematics, remained a source of confusion and debate. It was not until the development of calculus and the rigorous treatment of infinite sums that the paradox could be effectively resolved. Modern mathematical analysis demonstrates that while the number of intervals is indeed infinite, the sum of these intervals converges to a finite value, thereby allowing Achilles to eventually overtake the tortoise. Thus, what was once a profound antinomy has been relegated to a flawed argument, rooted in a misunderstanding of the nature of infinity. One of the primary issues is the low inter-rater reliability among human classifiers, which underscores the subjective nature of what constitutes hate speech. This subjectivity is further exacerbated by the use of misspellings, abbreviations, and other linguistic manipulations employed by individuals to evade detection. These tactics not only confound automated systems but also highlight the need for more sophisticated natural language processing (NLP) techniques that can recognize and interpret such variations. Another significant challenge is the dual use of keywords. Terms that may be considered benign in one context can be highly offensive in another, depending on the social and cultural milieu. For instance, a word or phrase that is innocuous in one community might carry a deeply pejorative connotation in another. This contextual dependency necessitates a nuanced understanding of the text, requiring NLP models to be sensitive to the broader sociocultural landscape in which the speech is embedded. The evolving nature of language and social phenomena adds another layer of complexity. Racial and minority insults, for example, are not static; they evolve over time, often in response to shifting social norms and political climates. This dynamic nature makes it difficult for static models to keep pace, necessitating continuous updates and retraining. Moreover, the use of sarcasm and irony, which can invert the literal meaning of a statement, further complicates the task of accurate detection. Sarcasm, in particular, requires a deep understanding of the speaker's intent, which is a challenging problem even for state-of-the-art NLP models. In addition to these complexities, the imprecise definitions of abusive language pose a significant hurdle. The lack of clear, universally accepted criteria for what constitutes hate speech versus other forms of abusive language can lead to inconsistent annotations and, consequently, to poorly trained models. text: The phenomenon of reduced individual effort in group settings, often referred to as social loafing, has been a subject of considerable interest in social psychology. Harkins and Jackson (1985) proposed that individuals tend to diminish their contributions in group contexts as a means of maintaining perceived equity. This behavior is driven by the assumption that other group members will also reduce their efforts, thereby justifying one's own diminished contribution. This perspective highlights the role of mutual expectations and the desire for fairness in the dynamics of group work. Kerr and Bruun (1983) further elaborated on this concept, introducing the notion of free-rider behavior, where individuals exert less effort because they believe their contributions are negligible. This form of behavior is characterized by a strategic reduction in effort, with the expectation that others will compensate for the shortfall. However, Hogg and Vaughan (2005) made a critical distinction between social loafing and free-riding. Social loafing involves making minimal contributions, while free-riding entails no contribution at all. This differentiation underscores the varying degrees of disengagement and the different motivations behind them. The self-efficacy theory offers another lens through which to understand these phenomena. According to this theory, individuals are likely to show lower effort when they perceive their self-efficacy, or belief in their ability to perform, as low. This is particularly true if they anticipate that their contributions will not be individually evaluated, thus reducing the incentive to exert maximum effort. The lack of personal accountability in a group setting can exacerbate this effect, as the collective nature of the task dilutes the sense of personal responsibility. Additionally, Mullen's (1983) self-attention hypothesis posits that working in a group can lead to a loss of self-awareness. In a group, individuals may feel less visible and accountable, leading to a decline in effort. Conversely, when working alone, individuals maintain a higher level of self-awareness, which can enhance productivity and effort. This hypothesis suggests that the structure of the work environment, and the extent to which it fosters self-awareness, plays a crucial role in determining the level of individual engagement.

Aquinas argues that truth, in its most proper sense, resides in the divine intellect, which serves as the eternal archetype of all created realities. Human cognition and material things, by contrast, participate in truth derivatively, to the extent that they mirror this perfect exemplar. This hierarchical conception of truth underscores the metaphysical foundation of Aquinas’s epistemology, wherein the divine exemplar serves as the ultimate measure of all intelligibility. Consequently, human knowledge, despite its limitations, attains truth when it mirrors, however imperfectly, the eternal wisdom of the divine intellect. text: The perennial inquiry into the mechanisms of language acquisition has yielded two profoundly divergent theoretical frameworks: the Behaviorist and the Cognitive-Nativist paradigms. These schools of thought offer contrasting epistemological underpinnings regarding how human beings come to master the intricate complexities of their native tongue. The Behaviorist theory, significantly advanced by Leonard Bloomfield, posits language as an essentially automatic human behavior, firmly rooted in the principles of stimulus and response. Within this framework, the infant mind is conceptualized as a tabula rasa, a blank slate upon which linguistic knowledge is inscribed through environmental interaction. Acquisition is thus viewed as a process of habit formation, where vocalizations that elicit positive reinforcement are strengthened and integrated into the speaker's repertoire, while unreinforced or negatively reinforced sounds eventually fade. This model emphasizes the crucial roles of listening, direct teaching, repetitive practice, and imitation in the child's linguistic development, aligning with broader behaviorist principles that prioritize observable phenomena and conditioning over internal cognitive states. Conversely, the Cognitive-Nativist theory, primarily championed by Noam Chomsky since its conceptualization in 1957, emerged as a potent critique of the behaviorist perspective, which Chomsky deemed superficial in its explanatory power. This paradigm asserts that language acquisition is not merely a product of environmental conditioning but rather a brain-centered process, underpinned by an innate, biologically endowed capacity. Infants, according to Chomsky, are born not as blank slates but with an inherent knowledge of Universal Grammar – a set of abstract linguistic principles common to all human languages. This innate facility, rather than extensive learning and practice alone, is posited to account for the remarkable speed, accuracy, and creativity with which children acquire language, even amidst impoverished and inconsistent linguistic input. Language, in this view, is fundamentally an innate mental faculty, a testament to humanity's unique cognitive architecture.

Among the most prevalent moves are those that state the purpose of the study, summarize critical findings, propose novel approaches or theoretical contributions, describe data and methodology, and provide an overview of the content. These elements often converge in a strategic manner, facilitating both comprehension and engagement for readers across diverse academic communities. A closer examination reveals that some moves are considered obligatory across fields. For instance, explicitly stating the study's purpose and summarizing key results are nearly indispensable components, serving as anchors that guide readers through the abstract’s narrative. By contrast, moves such as proposing innovative frameworks or drawing upon specific theories are quasi-obligatory, appearing less universally but still functioning as valuable tools for building academic discourse, especially in fields that emphasize theoretical innovation. Furthermore, abstract composition frequently demonstrates the interplay of multiple moves within the same text, as seen in the co-occurrence of "state purpose(s)" and "propose a new approach. " This interconnectedness not only reinforces the clarity of the abstract but also deepens its relevance for targeted audiences. Disciplinary variations in abstract structure further enrich the genre, yet a shared tendency persists to conclude by emphasizing content, practical implications, or opportunities for future research. Ultimately, the abstract serves as both an informative and indicative snapshot, harmonizing theoretical rigor with communicative accessibility.

Feelings of guilt and insecurity surrounding past sexually transmitted diseases (STDs) are commonly reported, as women often fear potential harm to their reproductive systems even years later. These concerns, compounded by lingering social taboos around sexual health, remain deeply personal and are rarely shared, even with loved ones. Such silence highlights a broader cultural discomfort with addressing women’s reproductive health openly, perpetuating cycles of shame and misunderstanding. In addition to these concerns, many women experience uncertainty from changes in their menstrual patterns. These changes—whether irregular cycles, heavier or lighter flows, or skipped periods—often leave women questioning whether their experiences are natural stages of life, indicative of aging, or precursors to menopause. Hesitancy to consult medical professionals about such changes is a common thread, driven in part by the fear of either discovering a serious issue or being dismissed altogether. This reluctance underscores the importance of fostering a more accessible and empathetic healthcare environment where women feel empowered to discuss these shifts without judgment. Attitudes toward menopause itself vary widely, shaped by personal experiences and cultural narratives surrounding aging and fertility. For some, menopause represents liberation—a welcome release from the physical and emotional burdens of menstruation and contraception. For others, however, it is an unwelcome marker of aging, bringing with it a perceived loss of vitality, desirability, and purpose tied to reproductive potential. Even among those for whom menopause is a distant concern, the anticipation of this transition often generates anxiety about its implications for identity and self-worth. Existing methods to evaluate BER are often constrained by trade-offs between accuracy and computational efficiency. For instance, Monte Carlo simulations remain the gold standard for detailed fault modeling due to their ability to capture intricate behaviors, but they are computationally infeasible for large-scale circuits. On the other hand, Statistical Static Timing Analysis (SSTA) excels in efficiently modeling timing variability but falls short of quantifying circuit-wide BER. To bridge this gap, this study introduces a novel methodology that combines practicality with rigor, improving the estimation of BER in digital circuits. The proposed approach employs probability density functions (PDFs) to statistically model transient faults, representing voltage variations at both gate inputs and outputs. By adopting this statistical representation, the model eliminates the need for extensive Monte Carlo iterations, thereby reducing computational burden while retaining a high degree of accuracy. This modular design simplifies the complexity of the analysis and facilitates a more manageable assessment of error dynamics. Overall, the approach presents a significant step forward in the effort to reliably estimate BER, combining statistical modeling with architectural insights. text: The Circulation and Imitation of Roman Republican Coinage in the Middle Danube Valley: Evidence from the Gomolava Hoard The middle Danube valley and eastern Romania have yielded a significant corpus of imitative Roman republican coinage, providing valuable insights into the economic and political interactions between Rome and the indigenous populations of the region during the late 2nd and early 1st centuries BCE. These imitations closely replicate the iconography and inscriptions of original Roman issues, particularly those minted in Macedonia and Greek colonies along the Black Sea. Common motifs include the helmeted head of Roma on the obverse and the biga (two-horse chariot) on the reverse, though the copies often exhibit minor deviations in design and legend execution, indicative of local minting practices. One of the most compelling archaeological contexts for studying these imitations is the late La Tène settlement layer at Gomolava, which dates to approximately 10 BCE and is associated with Tiberius’s military campaigns against the Scordisci. The destruction layer, marked by evidence of fire, contained not only imitative coinage but also genuine Roman denarii, including issues struck under Julius Caesar. This assemblage suggests a dual phenomenon of coin circulation: while official Roman currency entered the region through military and administrative channels, local copies simultaneously circulated, likely meeting the demand for transactional media in areas where official coinage was scarce. The presence of these imitations underscores the broader economic impact of Rome’s encroachment into Pannonia. Following the Roman occupation, the influx of both official and imitative currency signals heightened commercial activity, facilitated by the integration of the region into broader trade networks. Furthermore, the Gomolava hoard provides critical evidence for the monetization of local economies, reflecting not only the imposition of Roman economic structures but also the adaptive strategies of indigenous populations. By analyzing these coinages, scholars can better understand the intersection of imitation and authority in the monetized frontier zones of the early Roman Empire.

text: Gothic and Renaissance architecture, along with the modernist movement, represent three pivotal epochs in architectural history, each embodying distinct structural and aesthetic paradigms. Gothic architecture, which flourished from the 12th to the 16th century, is renowned for its verticality and ethereal brilliance, achieved through innovations such as ribbed vaults, pointed arches, and flying buttresses. These elements facilitated the redistribution of structural loads, enabling the construction of soaring cathedrals with expansive, light-filled clerestory windows adorned with intricate tracery. Additionally, decorative features like fan vaults and clustered piers exemplified the Gothic fascination with ornamental complexity, aspiring to evoke a sense of celestial grandeur. In contrast, Renaissance architecture, emerging in 15th-century Italy, marked a decisive return to classical ideals, emphasizing symmetry, proportion, and geometry inspired by ancient Roman and Greek principles. Architects such as Brunelleschi and Alberti championed the use of domes, cupolas, and statues, integrating humanist philosophy with structural innovation. The Renaissance sought harmonization between mathematical precision and aesthetic beauty, a stark departure from the Gothic emphasis on vertical aspiration. The modernist movement of the 20th century further revolutionized architectural thought by prioritizing functionality and minimalism. Rejecting ornamental excess, modernism embraced industrial materials—steel, glass, and reinforced concrete—to create structures defined by clean lines, open spaces, and efficiency. Figures like Le Corbusier and Mies van der Rohe advocated for the principle of "form follows function, " reshaping urban landscapes to reflect contemporary technological and social values. Collectively, these architectural movements illustrate the dynamic interplay between cultural ideals, technological advancements, and artistic expression, each leaving an indelible mark on the built environment.

At low reflectivity values, particularly between -10 dBZ and 5 dBZ, the TDF exhibits a significant increase, indicating a rapid decorrelation of signals. This phenomenon suggests weaker weather conditions characterized by sparse, irregularly distributed hydrometeors, where noise and atmospheric interference dominate the radar returns. The diminished particle concentration and erratic movement contribute to the pronounced decorrelation, making signal stability highly variable. As reflectivity intensifies within the moderate range of 5 dBZ to 40 dBZ, the TDF stabilizes, progressively approaching 100%. The enhancement in signal correlation is attributed to higher hydrometeor concentrations and more uniform velocity distributions within precipitating systems. Under these conditions, the increased density and motion coherence of particles—whether raindrops, snowflakes, or hailstones—reinforce the temporal correlation of the radar echoes, mitigating disruptive noise effects. Further investigation examines the cross-polar decorrelation time (DTτxy), which assesses polarization-dependent signal coherence. By applying curve-fitting techniques to radar data obtained from vertical transmit and horizontal receive (VH) polarization states, researchers model the interplay between reflectivity and DTτxy. The decorrelation time, derived from magnitude analysis, demonstrates distinct behavioral trends: tighter correlation in high-reflectivity conditions and greater variability in weaker echoes. These findings underscore the sensitivity of time decorrelation to precipitation intensity and microstructure.

In medieval Livonia, domestic animals were local in origin; there is no information that would suggest that livestock was brought in for animal breeding. The way animals were kept also affected the quality of the meat. In medieval times, domestic animals were outside for longer; these free-range beasts had to withstand the elements, which made them smaller in size, and tougher (Maldre 2003). Beef, goats, and sheep were not raised solely for meat and this influenced their slaughtering age, which in turn affected the quality of the meat. Only pigs were considered to be purely meat-animals, but they were to be slaughtered only when the optimal weight of the animal had been achieved. The importance of the pig as a source of meat and pork products in commerce is illustrated by information in medieval written sources on the butchering and dividing of the meat carcass of the pig – there is no such information on other animals (Põltsam-Jürjo 2017, 13). Ham was a big piece of pork from a back leg cut that was salted and smoked. Each pig, therefore, provided two hams. Pork ham was an important trade item, but people also prepared it at home for domestic consumption. Each animal offered two flitches (side speckes), and for long-term preservation, these were also salted and smoked. This fatty side of pork was the most popular ration; for example, in Inna Põltsam-Jürjo 45 1451, there were 100 flitches in the part of Lihula Castle belonging to the Livonian branch of the Teutonic Order (LUB 11: 160). Written sources also mention pork back (swins ruggen), which was obtained as a single piece from each animal. Pig’s trotters, head, and offal – everything was to be eaten. In medieval times, people tried to improve the quality of meat in several ways. Fattened and/or neutered animals and birds provided fattier, juicier, and more flavorful meat.

Further research is essential to refine printing speeds, enhance material properties, and streamline the CAD-to-production pipeline. Addressing these limitations will be critical in transitioning 3D-printed orthopedic solutions from experimental prototypes to mainstream medical applications, ultimately improving patient outcomes through personalized, high-performance immobilization devices.

text: The serpent motif, particularly the Ouroboros—a serpent consuming its own tail—occupies a significant position in ancient Egyptian mythology and iconography, embodying cyclical notions of time, renewal, and eternity. This symbol first appears with striking prominence in the tomb of Tutankhamun (14th century BCE), where it underscores the pharaonic belief in cosmic continuity and the afterlife. In this context, the Ouroboros functioned as a metaphysical boundary, simultaneously marking destruction and rebirth, a duality deeply embedded in Egyptian cosmological thought. During the Greco-Roman Period (332 BCE–395 CE), Egyptian astronomical and mythological imagery underwent a profound transformation with the incorporation of zodiacal representations influenced by Greek and Babylonian traditions. The Ptolemaic rulers facilitated the synthesis of Hellenistic astrology with indigenous Egyptian cosmology, leading to the widespread adoption of zodiacal motifs in temple frescoes, tomb ceilings, and ceremonial artifacts. Notably, the Dendera Zodiac from the Temple of Hathor epitomizes this mingling of traditions, illustrating celestial deities alongside Egyptian constellations in a highly syncretic artistic style. By the 2nd–3rd centuries CE, the serpent motif—initially a purely Egyptian symbol—had evolved into a standardized icon within this hybrid astronomical framework. No longer confined to its earlier mythic role, the Ouroboros began to function as a celestial emblem, representing planetary cycles and astral recurrence. This transition exemplifies how Egyptian art and cosmology dynamically adapted to external influences while retaining core symbolic structures, ensuring the endurance of these motifs well into late antiquity and beyond.

text: Evaluation of Electronic Component Performance Under High-Frequency Signal Interference This study investigates the susceptibility of electronic components to high-frequency (HF) electromagnetic interference, specifically high-power microwave (HPM) and ultra-wideband (UWB) signals exceeding 100 MHz. The research focuses on analyzing the vulnerability of a designated device under test (DUT) by monitoring its current response alongside that of an accompanying oscillator, revealing critical insights into performance degradation under electromagnetic stress. Experiments demonstrated consistent and reproducible results across identical component samples, yet significant variations were observed between units sourced from different manufacturers. One notable finding was the presence of a memory effect in the DUT when subjected to voltage levels below the established single-shot threshold, suggesting residual impacts of electromagnetic exposure even after initial interference events. The experimental setup employed a 7400-type CMOS oscillator as a control mechanism for the DUT, with HF-generator pulses inductively coupled into the signal line. However, coupling efficiency exhibited nonlinear behavior, particularly due to fluctuating input impedance in the DUT, which became more pronounced during voltage-induced operational upsets. These irregularities highlight the challenges in predicting electromagnetic interference effects in practical applications. The implications of this research extend to the enhancement of electromagnetic protection protocols for sensitive electronic systems. By elucidating the mechanisms of component vulnerability, this study provides a foundation for developing robust shielding and mitigation strategies against emerging electromagnetic threats. Further exploration into semiconductor-specific responses and variability between manufacturers is recommended to refine protective measures. (Correspondence: N.
